This paper introduces the TVP-Ar model, a novel method for modeling time series data that incorporates both observed data and explanatory variables, which are termed covariates in this context. Within the covariance stationary framework, the autoregressive coefficient is represented as a linear function of the covariates, while the integer-valued noise variance is modeled as a linear function of the covariates. The prior distribution for the intercept in the noise variance is set as a Beta distribution, and the prior for the slope is chosen as a Gamma distribution. Additionally, hyperparameters are defined to ensure the intercept remains positive and the variance stays within the range of zero to one. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed TVP-Ar model outperforms existing models in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the practical utility of this model is illustrated using a real-world air quality dataset. The results indicate that the TVP-Ar model effectively captures the temporal dynamics of the dataset and produces accurate predictions. The utility of this model for real-time forecasting is also highlighted in the context of a smart city framework. While astronomers employ photometry to measure the light blocked by exoplanets during transits for atmospheric analysis, meteorologists utilize identical techniques to assess how sunlight passes through atmospheric aerosols. This application, known as the Sun Photometry Method (SPM), has recently seen significant development. In this work, we identify errors in current SPM data reduction pipelines and demonstrate their impact on scientific conclusions using laboratory-generated aerosols. Specifically, we reveal that neglecting super-refraction—a phenomenon where the atmosphere acts like a lens, concentrating sunlight onto detectors—introduces significant mistakes. Additionally, we highlight errors stemming from the assumption of plane-parallel radiative transfer, which fails to hold true for strong aerosol layers when low phase functions are present. By integrating a radiative transfer model that accounts for both super-refraction and oblique ray paths, we present a novel method for quantifying aerosol optical depth (AOD) that achieves higher precision than existing approaches. Our results show that current methods underestimate AOD when it exceeds 1.0, whereas our new technique maintains high accuracy across all AOD levels. These findings indicate that recent studies reporting low AOD values in the upper atmosphere may be influenced by reduction errors, and we provide guidance for optimizing measurements in such conditions. Open-source code implementing our method is accessible at https://github.com/robcohn/SPM. Furthermore, meteorologists should note that errors associated with assuming no light scattering onto the detector during the Sun's rise and set are minimal compared to other sources of uncertainty. Our new method offers the highest precision yet for determining atmospheric aerosol properties, potentially transforming how meteorologists monitor and forecast aerosol-related air quality issues. Moreover, the approach could enable astronomers to push the limits of photometric precision for astronomical observations.

Current evaluations of image description generation rely on comparing textual outputs against human-written references. This approach assumes that reference texts are neutral, accurate accounts of the image content. However, existing datasets, including Caruso et al. (2019) and Miculicich et al. (2017), are known to contain errors and biases (Baumgartner et al., 2016; Goyal et al., 2017). These flaws can unfairly penalize state-of-the-art systems for failing to replicate biased or incorrect wording found in the data. To address this, we introduce a novel metric that evaluates image descriptions by assessing the semantic accuracy of a generated text relative to a human reference, rather than demanding exact linguistic alignment. Using existing datasets, we collected 1,000 samples per dataset to manually train and validate this new metric. When applied to standard description tasks on both datasets, this metric rewards models for correcting errors present in the references. Furthermore, when used as a reward function in a neural image description model, it guided the model toward generating more accurate descriptions, as confirmed by human evaluation. The source code and data required to reproduce this study are available at: https://github.com/anton-l/ABLE-Image-Description. We hope this metric encourages the development of image description systems that prioritize content accuracy over superficial linguistic similarities to flawed references. Ultimately, description generators—whether neural networks or human editors—should be assessed based on the factual correctness of their outputs relative to images, not on how closely they match potentially erroneous human captions.

This study presents a novel, nonperturbative framework for estimating the number of missing baryons and mesons required to achieve thermodynamic equilibrium during the hadronization of heavy-ion collisions. The method employs statistical hadronization models constrained by measured hadron yields, integrated over yields per unit rapidity across a wide range of species. These predictions align well with experimental data from relativistic heavy-ion collisions, including those at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Within this approach, hadron yields are determined by their single-particle spectral densities, which depend on temperature, chemical potential, and, crucially, the available baryon ($N_B$) and meson ($N_M$) degrees of freedom. These unknown quantities are solved for through fitting. Initially, analyses assume $N_B = N_M$ to derive a lower bound for the total extra hadons, yielding a value of $N_{tot} \approx 32$ per unit of baryon density ($\rho_B$). Subsequent work relaxes this constraint to explore scenarios where $N_M$ exceeds $N_B$. The results indicate that significant populations of exotic mesons, such as $D_s$ and $B_s$, are necessary to satisfy the data under this assumption. Furthermore, the findings support an approximately equal ratio of baryons to mesons, with $N_B/N_M$ falling between $0.8$ and $1.2$. Given that these results represent the first predictions derived from a fit to inclusive hadron yield data without introducing ad hoc modifications, they offer robust support for the canonical suppression mechanism as the cause of mass-dependent hadron yields observed in both $p$-Pb and heavy-ion collisions. Looking ahead, future applications of this method could involve other hadron production systems, such as Au-Au and Cu-Cu collisions at the SPS and RHIC, as well as Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions at the LHC. Additionally, once precise measurements of light hadron yields become available from the Future Circular Collider ( FCC-hh ), this approach could serve as a valuable tool for validating predictions from simulations of hadron gas dynamics in high-energy proton-proton and ion-ion collisions.

The Parton Distribution Function (PDF) forms the foundation of QCD calculations within parton distribution theory, enabling the prediction of hadronic collision outcomes. To optimize these predictions for specific applications, a user-friendly framework is required to guide PDF selection and modification. This process, known as fitting, involves aligning theoretical predictions with experimental data under a defined set of assumptions to derive the optimal function. While standard fitting methods yield a baseline distribution, specific applications often necessitate adjustments to this result. For instance, sideband regions utilized for signal extraction in B meson decays are typically not included in the original fit; consequently, post-fitting modifications in these areas are common. Similarly, when specific processes act as constraints in analyses involving differential cross-sections or decay rates, the resulting uncertainties may not fully capture the true variations possible in those variables. To systematically address such needs across various analyses, we have developed a framework allowing for customized PDF modifications tailored to individual requirements. Although no single approach is universally optimal, we propose a recommended workflow that ensures consistency between base and reweighted distributions, maintains isotropic uncertainty errors, and preserves the shape of charge asymmetries. To facilitate practical implementation, we integrated this methodology into the modern Monte Carlo routine for parton shower simulation and hadronization. We demonstrate its utility within the Belle II context through specific examples, providing a unified solution for both sideband variable constraints and sideband region fits. Furthermore, we applied this method to other Belle II analyses to explore the feasibility of incorporating additional process constraints and individual data points. Finally, we present the global fit result for the Belle II experiment, achieving a significant improvement in $\chi/\nu$ compared to the previous AYD (Amsler-Younghi-Delaunay) basis. This enhancement validates the utility of specialized analyses and the framework itself, confirming its value for future experiments as well. To support this, we open-sourced the code as the PYBFitter project at https://github.com/belle-pydata/PYBFitter. This study employs a linearized structural dynamics approach to investigate how an impinging jet fire responds to acoustic excitation driven by active flame dynamics. Utilizing Reynolds-averaged linearized equations, the work develops linear models for both the turbulent flow and reactive flow. Furthermore, a linear model is created to describe the structural vibrations. Finally, an optimization strategy is implemented to adjust the inlet velocity profiles along with the active flame distribution goals, aiming to maximize acoustic pressures at specific target locations or frequencies while simultaneously minimizing entropy generation. The model accounts for unsteady phenomena such as vortex shedding, which are exploited to create a linear model of the flow's circumferential velocity distribution. Simulations employ linear models of the flow, its vorticity, Reynolds stresses, and turbulent scalar fluxes, alongside the linearized structural and active flame models. These simulations optimize axial velocity profiles at inlets to enhance acoustic pressures at a target location and frequency, thereby exciting circumferential vortex shedding in the jet. Results indicate that UNsteady variations in circumferential velocity fluctuations significantly impact acoustic pressures at the target location. Additionally, the findings reveal that linear models of Reynolds stresses and turbulent scalar fluxes contribute meaningfully to predicting acoustic pressures, whereas those of turbulent scalar fluxes specifically play a crucial role in influencing velocity fluctuations at the target location. Lastly, it is observed that modifying the Reynolds stress anisotropy and the axial versus circumferential turbulent scalar flux anisotropy allows for altering acoustic pressures at the target location without changing the associated velocity fluctuations. These results suggest that future linear models of reactive flows should incorporate unsteady phenomena arising from mixing and enthalpy fraction distributions, such as circumferential turbulent fluctuations induced by inlet swirl. Such models could be integrated with nonlinear models of turbulence and scalar fluctuations to nonlinearly optimize inlet velocity distributions for creating "quiet" flames with low acoustic pressures at specific locations, potentially reducing structural vibrations and noise. Such nonlinear optimizations could also be guided by bio-inspired strategies, including prey-predator dynamics, pheromone trails, and bee swarm intelligence, to explore distributions that minimize acoustic pressures at a target location subject to constraints on total mass flow rate, mean Enthalpy Fraction anisotropy, and anisotropy of axial versus circumferential turbulent fluctuations. These optimizations might also consider linear models of structural vibrations to minimize oscillations caused by acoustic excitation at the target location. Such linear models would need to include unsteady reactive phenomena, which could nonlinearly interact with inlet velocity fluctuations to generate higher harmonic acoustic pressures

Nonlocal gravity theories extend action principles beyond local ones by incorporating nonlocal integral operators. These theories offer potential solutions to issues within classical gravitational theories and quantum field theories, such as the ultraviolet and infrared ultradivergences that arise in quantizing local action principles. This paper continues the development of a simple nonlocal extension of Einstein gravity, defined by the difference between two nonlocal operators acting on the Ricci tensor. We introduce an explicit formulation using constitutive connections that generalize the local Levi-Civita connection. This approach clarifies the nonlocal theory's dependence on geometric structures, analogous to how holographic theories rely on boundary geometry. Consequently, one can explore nonlocal gravity theories where the constitutive connection varies dynamically, adding further complexity to the model. We provide explicit expressions for these theories in terms of the Riemann tensor and other curvature invariants, highlighting that higher-order invariants become nonlocal. This formulation enables the investigation of such theories as effective field theories derived from more fundamental frameworks. We also present explicit forms for the bi-nonlocal operator in harmonic gauge and discuss its implications. Finally, we establish an identity for the bi-nonlocal operator under specific integral operator assumptions, facilitating the derivation of further properties.

This presentation reports on selected LHC experiments aimed at exploring the properties of tiny systems, which fall outside the traditional scope of heavy ion physics. Given that these systems are larger than any investigated by atomic or molecular physicists, we term them "mesoscopic." We outline several experimental campaigns that examine if phenomena typically associated with macroscopic, bulk matter emerge in these mesoscopic proton and ion collisions. Additionally, we highlight complementary theoretical and tabletop efforts required to assess the physical processes occurring within these miniature systems. Collectively, these initiatives represent a novel research direction at hadron facilities, potentially opening a new field of inquiry known as the physics of small systems. Furthermore, this area of research might find applications in the study of black hole formation.

The variable luminosity of X-ray binaries from the Galactic Centre has been steadily measured over the past two decades using the Timing Analysis Method. In contrast, for the binary system SAX J1808.4$-$36580 outside the Galactic Centre, we determined the luminosity variation by counting X-ray bursts and correlating this count with the previously established luminosity variation derived via the Timing Method for the same source. The resulting luminosity for SAX J1808.4$-$36580 aligns precisely with that obtained from the direct measurement used for the Galactic Centre binaries. Leveraging this consistency, we applied the count-based variability model to X-ray transient events recorded in the Galactic Centre, thereby estimating their luminosities. This estimation reveals that these transients exhibit greater variability than the non-active binaries from the same region, a finding that contradicts the hypothesis that such events represent sudden outbursts from dormant X-ray binaries. Furthermore, analyzing the repetition intervals of these transients, we propose that the neutron stars involved possess a previously unidentified population of Type-1 crustal cracks. Finally, we offer novel perspectives on the nature of X-ray binaries in the Galactic Centre.

Performance degradation techniques serve a dual role: they function as side-channel attacks complementing cache exploits like Prime+Probe, and as countermeasures masking original execution times to thwart Simple Timing Attacks. While effective, existing methods often fall short in granularity when confronting complex execution time side-channel models. We introduce HyperDegrade, a novel technique that surpasses prior limitations by executing the program under optimization at native speed and layering multiple degradation layers upon it. Evaluations using both real and simulated executions demonstrate that HyperDegrade achieves target frequencies of 2.0 GHz, representing a tenfold improvement over previous approaches. When applied to countermeasure side-channels, HyperDegrade enables a complete neutralization of execution time leakage. Furthermore, when utilized with execution time masking, it significantly amplifies the information gained from cache side-channels. We validate these findings across two distinct architectures: Intel and AMD. Ultimately, the integration of HyperDegrade with a program under optimization yields a net information loss, as programs executed at lower frequencies require longer durations to gather equivalent data. Our assessments confirm that this benefit is substantial, particularly when counteracted with further masking or when confronting more granular execution time models. Additionally, we establish new lower bounds for achievable frequencies, proving that HyperDegrade remains effective even when total leakage is minimized through the combination of execution time and cache side-channels. Finally, we outline future research directions needed to push these limits even lower. The source code and binary traces for our assessments are accessible at https://github.com/Anish-1999/HyperDegrade. Performance degradation strategies remain a dynamic battlefield, offering valuable capabilities as a side.

Because XL-MIMO base stations (BSs) offer such extensive service areas, a single visible BS often has sufficient capacity to accommodate all user equipments (UEs) within its range. Although neural networks have largely supplanted $N$-gram models in modern language technology due to their superior performance, recent research indicates that neural outputs often fail to align with human linguistic intuitions as measured by $N$-gram-based metrics. This study introduces a two-stage framework for neural text creation where the first stage leverages an out-of-domain $N$-gram language model, and the second stage employs a task-specific neural decoder. Experimental results from machine translation and summarization tasks demonstrate that this hybrid approach consistently outperforms both standalone neural and $N$-gram models. Specifically, the framework yields significant gains when evaluated with $N$-gram-based metrics, while maintaining comparable performance against standard neural metrics. These findings suggest that the limitations of certain evaluation metrics can bias assessments of system performance. Consequently, this research cautions against relying solely on point-based scores for metrics like BLEU when comparing systems with dissimilar characteristics, particularly when such scores guide selection. Metric dimension, a concept from geometry, is standardly defined using the distance function $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ between pairs of vertices. For graphs representing communication networks, this distance corresponds to the length of the shortest path. In such network contexts, it is both practical and necessary to consider an alternative to the traditional distance: the optimized distance function $d_+(\cdot,\cdot)$, which represents the minimum time required for information to travel between any two vertices via a dedicated edge. This paper introduces the notions of metric dimension and resolvability based on $d_+$. We demonstrate that for a wide range of graphs, determining the metric dimension under $d_+$ is equivalent to finding a minimum size resolving set where each vertex is resolved by at least three distinct vertices (or by a single vertex in specific cases) using the optimized distance. Furthermore, we define a "metric dimension" and "resolving dimension" for graphs that are not necessarily finite by employing measure theory. We establish upper and lower bounds for these dimensions as a function of the graph's order, and we prove that for almost all finite graphs, these dimensions converge to logarithmic growth relative to the graph's order. Additionally, we define the dimension of connectivity as the minimum order of a graph required to achieve a given dimension. Finally, we derive the dimension of dimensionality for several common graph families and specific regular graphs.

Furthermore, clinical adoption is difficult due to additive interference caused by background noise and by the deformation of acoustic waves resulting from variations in stethoscope placement and conduction paths. These results indicate that explicitly modeling acoustic wave deformation within a neural network architecture effectively improves categorization, particularly in multi-way classification tasks under multi-shot and zero-shot conditions. Ultimately, AID-Net has the potential to support cardiologists in detecting atypical heart abnormalities using acoustic stethoscope recordings. This study reports the unexpected contraction observed by TESS for the giant variable star $\kappa$ Carinae ($\kappa$ Crb), a phenomenon that appears too rapid to remain undetected by current literature. While previous work attributed this contraction to the spin-up of a convective envelope following the engulfment of a low-mass planet, our analysis indicates that the envelope's actual rotation speed is significantly lower than required for such spin-up. Alternatively, if the envelope is colder and heavier than previously thought, planet engulfment could still account for the observed spin-up; however, this would contradict standard stellar evolution models, which do not predict the necessary mass and temperature. We outline potential solutions to these challenges, such as unwinding the core to drive envelope spin-up via core-envelope coupling or engaging magnetic braking. Ultimately, the solution relies on revised mass and age estimates, implying that $\kappa$ Crb is younger and less evolved than currently believed. Regardless of the specific mechanism, the event serves as compelling evidence for planetary engulfment, though alternative explanations without planet involvement remain possible. Further investigation is required to confirm the cause, and we provide a simplified theoretical framework to guide future searches for similar contraction signals resulting from planetary absorption. Such contractions could act as a detectable signature of planet engulfment in other systems, although other causes for spin-up must first be ruled out. We conclude by discussing the implications of this evidence for angular momentum evolution in giant stars, potential detectability of planet engulfment post-engagement, and its relevance to the so-called "missing mass" of giant planets. Although the volume of fake news on social media platforms has recently decreased due to massive fact-checking initiatives, the potential for malicious actors to exploit counterfeit content for deceptive purposes remains significant. Creating fact-checked content for articles or blog posts remains a labor-intensive and costly endeavor, prompting industry professionals to explore automated detection systems. However, the inherently imbalanced nature of multimodal counterfeit news datasets, where verified samples are scarce, hinders the development of effective deep learning models. This challenge is particularly acute in specific domains where dataset sizes are limited. For instance, professional football (soccer) involves numerous entities such as teams, players, venues, and brands, yet relevant multimodal counterfeit news is both rare and constantly evolving. As illustrated in Figure 1, such content typically consists of a manipulated image—often generated via GANs—to mislead viewers, paired with an accompanying article. To address this, we propose \textbf{MECND}, a framework for detecting emergent counterfeit news that leverages the semantic meanings of image pixels, textual language, and meta data. Specifically, we employ a meta learning approach to formulate a game between a detector and sources of fake news, aiming to identify previously unseen manipulated image news. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, one German and one English, demonstrate that our framework effectively detects emergent counterfeit news without requiring task-specific training on those datasets. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by four folds on the German dataset and twice as effective on the English dataset. We address the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox using a setup that appears to exhibit nonlocal correlations, as illustrated in Figure 1. Furthermore, we show that this guidance effect becomes manifest only when the single-particle state exhibits genuine quantum behavior through interference. Crucially, we prove that this guidance cannot be accounted for if the particle's state is classical. This conclusion holds regardless of whether the particle's wavefunction is delocalized across a specific boundary or remains confined to a single location on one side of it. Consequently, this phenomenon represents a truly novel form of nonlocality arising from quantum superposition, a resource we suggest could enable remote quantum operations, such as reversing the direction of a localized particle's wavefunction at a distance. We also clarify why this resource remains underutilized in existing experiments. Additionally, we provide evidence that this nonlocality is inherently genuine, not merely apparent, by refuting explanations based on Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen underdetermination, steering, or entanglement monogamy. Notably, such nonlocality can be generated with truly single-particle entanglement, a resource we define and for which we outline potential applications, including enhanced energy extraction from thermal batteries and improved sensing of local field variations. Invariant manifolds, particularly linear ones, are fundamental for analyzing the local dynamics of dynamical systems near fixed points. The superposition of these manifolds creates a partition of phase space known as the "invariant surface structure." Within each region, the system exhibits specific local dynamics, which can be highly complex. This structure often gives rise to non-classical dynamics, such as a saddle-focus fixed point displaying both stable and unstable dynamics on its invariant surfaces, alongside homoclinic orbits and chaotic behavior on Poincaré sections—a phenomenon termed "invariant surface chaos." Such chaos is fundamentally distinct from Eulerian chaos, which emerges from chaotic attractors due to the coexistence of attracting and repelling periodic orbits. While invariant surface chaos has been extensively studied in continuous dynamical systems using numerical methods, a comprehensive theoretical investigation remains a significant challenge. This paper presents a unified theoretical framework for examining invariant surface chaos across various fractional-order continuous dynamical systems. Within this framework, we demonstrate that this type of chaos cannot occur in ultra-low dimensional systems. We also provide a detailed analysis of this phenomenon in the Lorenz system and its fractional-order counterparts. Our findings reveal that, contrary to common assumptions, the chaotic attractor in the chaotic regime of the Lorenz system is not an Eulerian chaotic attractor, and the system does not exhibit invariant surface chaos. These results carry important implications for the security applications of the Lorenz system and its fractional-order versions. Additionally, we offer a detailed discussion on the significance of these results for related research domains.

Engagement recordings, which consist of seismic data captured during atmospheric acoustic events, present significant inversion challenges due to limited bandwidth, sparsity, and noise. These issues are particularly acute in regions beyond the acoustic focus. Despite these difficulties, inversion remains essential for verifying the authenticity of such recordings and for initiating seismic waveform retrieval to identify the generating mechanism. This study utilizes the 1999 Nis atomic bomb detonation recordings as a case for inversion retrieval. Additionally, it examines the 2013 Chechen village airstrike recordings to validate the proposed method. Furthermore, the approach is applied to reconstruct and replay the 1982 Israeli village shelling recordings from the Khalisa incident. It is also used to retrieve and play back the waveform of the 2022 Ukrainian village artillery firing. Finally, the method reconstructs and audibly presents the waveform for the 1888 Italian volcanic explosion recorded by a barometric sensor. The proposed technique involves an iterative process: initially, an acoustic forward model is inverted to estimate a rough initial estimate of the source mechanism. Subsequently, a 3D numerical simulation based on the Born approximation is employed to refine and optimize the source mechanism, ultimately yielding a physically realistic mechanism. The inverted source mechanisms for each event are reconstructed and displayed as both spatial distributions of mechanism types and temporal evolutions of those types. Finally, the retrieved waveforms are superimposed onto the original recordings for residual analysis. The inverse problem is resolved through a customized Hierarchical Metropolis-Aspired Walk sampling algorithm. As demonstrated by the reconstructed residuals for all tested events, the initial events—whether caused by explosions, gunfire, or atmospheric shocks—align closely with the residuals, confirming the validity of the proposed method. These results indicate that even in severely limited scenarios, the 3D numerical model successfully reconstructed the source waveform of the 1888 Italian volcanic seismic acoustic event, revealing clear evidence of an explosive origin. Consequently, the initial inversions provide a valuable dataset for further analyzing the mechanisms of structural acoustic events. Such investigations can clarify misconceptions regarding the feasibility of constructing natural events that mimic specific seismic or atmospheric events to deceive intelligence systems or military operations. We introduce the simplest non-standard scoto-seesaw model featuring a linear-rainbow seesaw mechanism. This extended Standard Model includes three heavy right-handed neutrinos, one new scalar, and one new fermion, representing the minimal configuration required to elevate the seesaw scale to 100 TeV within this architectural framework. Notably, this model constitutes the simplest seesaw solution capable of stabilizing the Higgs vacuum against decay, even with heavy particle masses up to 100 TeV. We briefly examine the phenomenology of light neutral Higgs states, detailing the production and decay characteristics of the like-charged scalar pair. Furthermore, we present the parametric parameters required for generating neutral Higgs masses ranging from 200 GeV to 1 TeV within the 100 TeV scale regime, alongside an analysis of the production and decay behavior of its light charged scalar. Our investigation confirms that this model can serve as a viable dark matter candidate, operating effectively within the 100 TeV mass range. We specifically explore the phenomenology of its WIMP (weakly interacting massive particle) dark matter, focusing on its production and decay dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that this model offers the most straightforward weak-scale dark matter scenario in the simplest seesaw mechanism capable of stabilizing the Higgs vacuum at scales as high as 100 TeV. Additionally, we outline the physics potential of this model at future colliders, particularly at a 100 TeV proton-proton collision facility. Extensive simulation codes for both 100 TeV and 14 TeV proton-proton collision environments, covering processes from production to final detection, are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Xiao-QiangFU/Simplest-NS-Scoto-Seesaw_Model_. We conclude by suggesting potential experimental signatures observable at a 100 TeV proton-proton collider.
